passages.passage_text: Short stature in childhood has several endocrine causes. Growth hormone (GH) is released in pulses from anterior pituitary somatotrophs under the control of two hypothalamic peptides: GHRH, which stimulates release, and somatostatin, which inhibits it. GH acts on the liver and other tissues to raise insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which promotes bone growth and feeds back negatively on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary. Because GH secretion is pulsatile, a single random GH level is uninformative, so clinicians give a provocative stimulus (arginine) and measure peak GH. In some cases GHRH is also injected to test pituitary responsiveness. Three children with short stature were evaluated, and each was then treated with recombinant human GH (rhGH) for one year. Results are shown in Table 1. A normal peak GH after stimulation is above 10 ng/mL, and normal IGF-1 is defined as 100% of the age-matched mean. Children were measured at the same clinic with standard stadiometers.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.1 | 2.4 | 20 | 3.2 | 9.5 |
| 2 | 1.9 | 14.8 | 25 | 3.5 | 9.0 |

questions.stem: The results for Patient 1 are most consistent with a defect located in which structure?

options.A: The anterior pituitary somatotrophs, because they fail to release GH even when stimulated directly by GHRH
options.B: The hypothalamic neurons that secrete GHRH, because the pituitary would then respond normally to injected GHRH
options.C: The liver, because it cannot synthesize IGF-1 even though pituitary GH release is normal
options.D: The GH receptor on target tissues, because GH levels would then be high after stimulation

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Patient 1 has low GH after both arginine and GHRH, so the pituitary cannot respond even to direct GHRH stimulation; the pituitary is the site of the lesion. Why the others are wrong: B) Patient 2, not Patient 1, shows that pattern: a normal response to GHRH after a failed arginine response. C) Patient 1 has low GH, and a liver defect would give normal or high GH with low IGF-1. D) A receptor defect gives high GH, as in Patient 3; Patient 1 has low GH.
questions.trap: Choosing the hypothalamus because low GH after arginine looks like a hypothalamic problem, ignoring the failed GHRH response that localizes the defect to the pituitary.

questions.stem: Patient 3 has a high peak GH but a low IGF-1 level and does not grow in response to rhGH. The best explanation is

options.A: a defective GH receptor or post-receptor pathway, which prevents IGF-1 production and removes negative feedback on GH release
options.B: a deficiency of somatostatin, which would raise GH release but leave IGF-1 production and the growth response to rhGH completely normal
options.C: a pituitary tumor secreting GH autonomously, which would raise IGF-1 above the age norm
options.D: a deficiency of GHRH, which would give a low GH peak and a good growth response to rhGH

questions.explanation: Correct: A) High GH with low IGF-1 and no response to exogenous GH indicates the tissues cannot respond to GH; low IGF-1 then fails to feed back, so GH stays high. Why the others are wrong: B) Without somatostatin, GH is high, but receptors would still respond to it, so IGF-1 and rhGH response would be normal. C) An autonomous GH-secreting tumor gives high IGF-1 because the receptors are working. D) Low GHRH gives low GH, as in Patient 2, with a strong rhGH response.
questions.trap: Assuming that high GH must mean high IGF-1; the liver makes IGF-1 only if the GH receptor signals.

questions.stem: Why is serum IGF-1, rather than a random GH measurement, used to screen for GH deficiency?

options.A: GH is destroyed by the liver within seconds, so it can never be detected in plasma
options.B: IGF-1 is secreted in pulses that are larger than those of GH, which makes it easier to detect
options.C: IGF-1 is long-lived and stable, so it reflects GH secretion integrated over time
options.D: IGF-1 is produced by the pituitary itself, so it directly measures somatotroph mass

questions.explanation: Correct: C) GH is released in short pulses and cleared quickly, whereas IGF-1 is bound to carrier proteins and stays at a stable level that reflects average GH exposure. Why the others are wrong: A) GH has a short half-life (minutes) but is detectable; it is not destroyed within seconds. B) IGF-1 is not pulsatile; its stability is the reason it is useful. D) IGF-1 is made mainly by the liver in response to GH, not by the pituitary.
questions.trap: Believing IGF-1 is a pituitary hormone; it is a liver-derived (and locally produced) mediator of GH action.

questions.stem: If Patient 1 continues rhGH treatment, approximately how many additional centimeters will Patient 1 grow over two years compared with no treatment?

options.A: 6.3 cm
options.B: 9.5 cm

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Growth gain per year is 9.5 - 3.2 = 6.3 cm; over two years this is 2 x 6.3 = 12.6 cm. Why the others are wrong: A) 6.3 cm is the one-year gain, not the two-year gain. B) 9.5 cm is the on-treatment velocity for a single year, not the gain over the untreated rate. C) 19.0 cm is two years of total treated growth, not the difference from untreated growth.
questions.trap: Using the treated velocity directly instead of subtracting the untreated growth rate.

questions.stem: Which treatment would be most likely to improve growth in Patient 3?

options.A: Higher-dose rhGH, because overcoming a receptor defect only requires more ligand
options.B: Recombinant IGF-1, because it bypasses the nonfunctional GH receptor signaling that normally generates IGF-1
options.C: A GHRH analog, because GH release is the limiting step in this patient
options.D: Octreotide, a somatostatin analog, because it lowers the elevated GH and thereby corrects the growth failure of this child

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Patient 3 cannot make IGF-1 in response to GH, so supplying IGF-1 directly replaces the missing mediator. Why the others are wrong: A) The receptor pathway is defective, so more GH gives no extra benefit; Patient 3 already shows 2.1 cm/yr on rhGH. C) GH is already high after stimulation, so more GHRH adds nothing. D) Lowering GH further would not help; IGF-1 is the missing mediator, and octreotide would reduce a hormone that is not the problem.
questions.trap: Treating the elevated GH level rather than the missing IGF-1 effect.

passages.passage_text: Diuretics increase urinary salt and water excretion by inhibiting transporters along the nephron. In a crossover study, healthy volunteers on a fixed diet received a single oral dose of placebo, furosemide (a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter), hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ, which inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter), or spironolactone (an aldosterone receptor antagonist) on separate days. Urine was collected for 6 hours after each dose. Results are shown in Table 1. Assume that each volunteer had a glomerular filtration rate of 120 mL/min and a plasma sodium concentration of 140 mmol/L throughout the study, so that about 6,000 mmol of sodium was filtered during the 6 hours. Volunteers refrained from caffeine and alcohol for 24 hours, drank 500 mL of water 30 minutes before dosing, and remained seated during the collection period. Urine osmolality was measured by freezing-point depression, and electrolytes by ion-selective electrodes. Each treatment was separated by a one-week washout, and the order of treatments was randomized.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Placebo | 900 | 60 | 30 | 3.0 | 650 |
| Furosemide | 2800 | 250 | 60 | 7.5 | 300 |
| HCTZ | 1600 | 140 | 45 | 1.5 | 480 |
| Spironolactone | 1100 | 85 | 18 | 3.1 | 600 |

questions.stem: The fall in urine osmolality after furosemide is best explained by which effect?

options.A: Increased ADH secretion, which opens aquaporins in the collecting duct and dilutes the urine
options.B: Reduced solute reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, which collapses the medullary gradient that concentrates urine
options.C: Increased reabsorption of water in the proximal tubule, which concentrates the filtrate
options.D: Blockade of aldosterone receptors in principal cells, which raises water excretion without changing the gradient

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The thick ascending limb normally pumps NaCl out of the lumen to build the medullary interstitial gradient; blocking NKCC2 dissipates the gradient, so the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine. Why the others are wrong: A) More ADH would make urine more concentrated, not less. C) Proximal water reabsorption is not the target of furosemide, and it would reduce volume. D) Aldosterone antagonism is the mechanism of spironolactone and does not account for the furosemide result.
questions.trap: Attributing the dilute urine to the collecting duct rather than to loss of the medullary gradient from the loop of Henle.

questions.stem: Spironolactone lowers urinary K+ excretion below the placebo value because it

options.A: inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, which reduces K+ delivery to the distal nephron
options.B: blocks aldosterone-driven Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the principal cells of the collecting duct
options.C: inhibits the Na-Cl cotransporter, which raises distal flow and K+ secretion
options.D: inhibits proximal K+ reabsorption, which leaves more K+ in the tubular fluid

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Aldosterone increases ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase activity in principal cells; blocking its receptor reduces Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion, so K+ is retained. Why the others are wrong: A) Inhibiting NKCC2 is the action of furosemide, which increased K+ loss. C) NCC inhibition is the action of HCTZ, and it increased K+ excretion. D) Spironolactone does not act in the proximal tubule, and blocking K+ reabsorption would increase, not lower, K+ excretion.
questions.trap: Confusing the K+-sparing aldosterone antagonist with loop and thiazide diuretics, which raise K+ loss.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason that furosemide increased K+ excretion?

options.A: More Na+ and fluid reaching the collecting duct raises Na+ reabsorption through ENaC, which makes the lumen negative and drives K+ secretion
options.B: Furosemide directly opens K+ channels in the thick ascending limb, which lets K+ escape from the lumen into the urine, independent of any change in distal sodium delivery or tubular flow
options.C: Furosemide lowers plasma aldosterone, which reduces K+ reabsorption in the distal nephron
options.D: Furosemide inhibits H+/K+-ATPase in intercalated cells, which removes K+ reabsorption

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Greater distal delivery of Na+ and high tubular flow increase Na+ entry via ENaC and sweep secreted K+ away, so K+ excretion rises. Why the others are wrong: B) Furosemide acts on NKCC2; it does not open K+ channels, and K+ secretion occurs mainly in the collecting duct. C) Furosemide tends to raise renin and aldosterone through volume depletion, which also contributes to K+ loss. D) Inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase is not the mechanism of furosemide, and that pump mediates K+ reabsorption of minor extent.
questions.trap: Looking for a direct effect of the drug on K+ transport instead of the downstream effect of increased distal flow and sodium delivery.

questions.stem: Under furosemide, the fractional excretion of sodium (Na+ excreted divided by Na+ filtered) was approximately
questions.explanation: Correct: A) Filtered Na+ is about 6,000 mmol, and 250 / 6,000 is approximately 0.042, or about 4%. Why the others are wrong: B) 1% is the placebo value (60 / 6,000), not the furosemide value. C) 10% would require about 600 mmol of Na+ in the urine. D) 42% results from dividing by 600 mmol instead of 6,000 mmol.
questions.trap: Dividing by the wrong filtered load or using the placebo excretion.

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent calcium kidney stones and high urinary calcium would be best treated with which drug, based on Table 1?

options.A: Furosemide, because it increases urine volume the most and dilutes urinary calcium
options.B: Spironolactone, because it has the largest effect on Na+ excretion of the drugs tested
options.C: Placebo, because none of the drugs changes Ca2+ excretion in a clinically useful direction
options.D: HCTZ, because it lowers urinary Ca2+ excretion below the placebo value

questions.explanation: Correct: D) HCTZ reduced Ca2+ excretion from 3.0 to 1.5 mmol, consistent with enhanced distal Ca2+ reabsorption, lowering supersaturation and stone risk. Why the others are wrong: A) Furosemide more than doubled Ca2+ excretion (7.5 mmol), which would worsen stone formation despite higher volume. B) Spironolactone did not change Ca2+ excretion (3.1 mmol) and had the smallest Na+ effect among the drugs. C) HCTZ clearly lowered Ca2+ excretion, so the claim that none of the drugs changes it is incorrect.
questions.trap: Choosing the diuretic with the greatest volume effect without checking the calcium column.

passages.passage_text: Lactase, a brush-border enzyme of the small intestine, hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. In most mammals and in many human populations, lactase activity declines after weaning (lactase non-persistence). Unabsorbed lactose passes to the colon, where bacteria ferment it. A hydrogen breath test detects this process. After an overnight fast, adults drank 50 g of lactose in water, and breath hydrogen was measured over 3 hours (Figure 1). Participants were lactase-persistent, lactase-nonpersistent, or lactase-nonpersistent after taking an oral lactase supplement with the lactose. Jejunal biopsy lactase activity, the rise in blood glucose after 50 g of lactose, and stool pH measured the next morning were also recorded (Table 1). Participants avoided high-fiber foods and antibiotics for the preceding four weeks, since both can change the colonic flora, and did not smoke or exercise during testing because these affect breath hydrogen. Symptoms were scored by questionnaire, and each test was performed on a separate day in randomized order.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lactase-persistent | 40 | 30 | 6 | 6.8 |
| Lactase-nonpersistent | 4 | 4 | 70 | 5.4 |
| Nonpersistent + lactase supplement | 4 | 24 | 15 | 6.5 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Breath hydrogen after 50 g lactose

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the small blood glucose rise in the lactase-nonpersistent group?

options.A: Lactose cannot be absorbed intact, so with little brush-border lactase there is little glucose and galactose available for uptake
options.B: Lactase-nonpersistent intestinal cells lack the SGLT1 transporter, so no glucose from any source can be absorbed and the lactose-derived sugars stay in the lumen
options.C: The liver converts all absorbed glucose to glycogen before it reaches the blood
options.D: Colonic bacteria consume the glucose released by lactase before it can be absorbed

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Disaccharides must be hydrolyzed at the brush border before monosaccharide transporters can absorb them; low lactase activity limits glucose release from lactose. Why the others are wrong: B) The supplement group absorbed glucose normally, so transporters are intact; only the enzyme is deficient. C) Hepatic glycogen synthesis would not eliminate the rise in the first hour and does not distinguish the groups. D) The bacteria act in the colon, after the main site of absorption, and ferment unabsorbed lactose rather than glucose already hydrolyzed.
questions.trap: Assuming a transporter defect rather than a missing hydrolase step.

questions.stem: In the lactase-nonpersistent group, breath hydrogen rose substantially only after about 60 minutes. The best explanation is that

options.A: the small intestine produces hydrogen gas only after prolonged exposure to lactose
options.B: lactose must first be converted to galactose in the liver and then metabolized by hepatocytes, which releases hydrogen into the blood
options.C: pancreatic enzymes produce hydrogen slowly as they digest lactose in the duodenum
options.D: unabsorbed lactose first has to travel to the colon, where bacteria ferment it and release hydrogen that is absorbed and exhaled

questions.explanation: Correct: D) H2 is a product of bacterial fermentation, and the colonic bacteria need the lactose to arrive from the small intestine, which takes time. Why the others are wrong: A) Human cells do not generate hydrogen from lactose; bacteria do. B) Hydrogen arises from colonic fermentation, not hepatic metabolism of galactose. C) Pancreatic enzymes do not digest lactose, and they do not produce hydrogen.
questions.trap: Attributing hydrogen production to human digestion instead of bacterial fermentation.

questions.stem: The lower stool pH in the lactase-nonpersistent group most likely reflects

options.A: short-chain fatty acids and lactic acid produced when colonic bacteria ferment unabsorbed lactose
options.B: increased bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas in response to lactose
options.C: bile acids that are not reabsorbed in the ileum and that acidify the stool
options.D: gastric acid that is not neutralized because lactose delays gastric emptying

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Bacterial fermentation of lactose produces organic acids, which lower fecal pH to 5.4 and also generate gas. Why the others are wrong: B) Bicarbonate secretion would raise, not lower, the pH. C) Unreabsorbed bile acids can cause diarrhea but are not the cause here and do not account for the supplement effect. D) Gastric acid is neutralized in the duodenum by bicarbonate and does not set stool pH.
questions.trap: Choosing an upper GI explanation for a colonic finding.

questions.stem: Lactase-nonpersistent individuals often develop watery diarrhea after consuming lactose. The most direct cause is that unabsorbed lactose

options.A: raises the osmolarity of luminal contents and holds water in the intestine
options.B: activates adenylyl cyclase in the crypt cells and drives active Cl- secretion
options.C: damages the intestinal villi and thereby reduces the surface area for absorption
options.D: stimulates gastrin release, which increases motility throughout the small intestine

questions.explanation: Correct: A) An unabsorbed, osmotically active solute draws water into the lumen, an osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting or lactose avoidance. Why the others are wrong: B) Cl- secretion driven by cAMP is the mechanism of cholera toxin, not of lactose malabsorption. C) Lactase non-persistence is not associated with villous damage; the mucosa is normal. D) Lactose does not stimulate gastrin to an appreciable degree, and increased motility is not the main mechanism.
questions.trap: Linking lactose to secretory diarrhea rather than to the osmotic effect of unabsorbed solute.

questions.stem: Peak breath hydrogen in lactase-nonpersistent participants was how many times that of participants who took the supplement?

options.A: About 0.2
options.B: About 11.7
options.C: About 4.7
options.D: About 55

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Peak H2 was 70 ppm without the supplement and 15 ppm with it, so 70 / 15 is approximately 4.7. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.2 is the reciprocal (15 / 70). B) 11.7 is the ratio of the nonpersistent peak to the lactase-persistent peak (70 / 6). D) 55 is the difference in ppm (70 - 15), not a ratio.
questions.trap: Computing a difference instead of a ratio, or using the wrong comparison group.

passages.passage_text: Ovulation requires a surge of luteinizing hormone (LH). During most of the menstrual cycle, estradiol from the ovarian follicles suppresses GnRH and gonadotropin release (negative feedback), but late in the follicular phase high estradiol switches to positive feedback and triggers the LH surge. To test the conditions for this switch, researchers infused estradiol at a constant concentration into women in the early follicular phase whose own ovarian steroid output had been suppressed, and measured serum LH over 72 hours (Figure 1). One infusion maintained serum estradiol at 50 pg/mL and the other at 250 pg/mL. Table 1 summarizes typical hormone and endometrial values across the natural cycle in other volunteers. Estradiol was measured by immunoassay, and LH by a two-site immunometric assay. Ultrasound confirmed that no dominant follicle was developing at the start of each infusion, and each woman received both concentrations in separate cycles, in randomized order. Values in Table 1 are means from regularly cycling women.

questions.stem: The results for the 50 pg/mL infusion are best explained by

options.A: positive feedback by estradiol, which raises LH release as soon as the concentration exceeds a fixed threshold in the pituitary
options.B: direct inhibition of the ovary by LH, which lowers estradiol production
options.C: negative feedback by estradiol on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, which lowers GnRH and LH release
options.D: stimulation of the corpus luteum, which secretes inhibin and lowers LH

questions.explanation: Correct: C) A modest, sustained estradiol level suppressed LH from 6 to about 4.5 mIU/mL, the signature of negative feedback. Why the others are wrong: A) Positive feedback was seen only at 250 pg/mL after about 36 hours. B) LH acts on the ovary rather than being inhibited by it, and estradiol was fixed by the infusion. D) The women were in the follicular phase with no corpus luteum.
questions.trap: Predicting a surge at any estradiol level instead of recognizing that both concentration and duration determine the feedback direction.

questions.stem: In the natural cycle, the rapid rise in estradiol late in the follicular phase is produced mainly by

options.A: theca cells of the corpus luteum, which convert progesterone to estradiol under the control of LH during the follicular phase
options.B: granulosa cells of the dominant follicle, which use aromatase to convert androgens made by theca cells
options.C: the anterior pituitary, which secretes estradiol in response to GnRH
options.D: the adrenal medulla, which converts cortisol to estradiol

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Under FSH stimulation, granulosa cells express aromatase and convert thecal androgens to estradiol; the dominant follicle becomes the main source. Why the others are wrong: A) No corpus luteum exists in the follicular phase, and the luteal source is secondary. C) The pituitary secretes FSH and LH, not estradiol. D) The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines, not sex steroids.
questions.trap: Assigning estradiol synthesis to theca cells alone, which make androgens but lack significant aromatase.

questions.stem: In the mid-luteal phase, FSH and LH are low (3 and 4 mIU/mL). Which explanation fits the data in Table 1?

options.A: Low progesterone removes inhibition of the hypothalamus, which lowers GnRH release
options.B: High FSH from the developing follicle inhibits its own secretion through a short-loop pathway that involves the endometrium and uterine tubes
options.C: High progesterone, together with estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum, suppresses gonadotropin secretion by negative feedback
options.D: The endometrium secretes LH-suppressing factors when it reaches 12 mm

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Progesterone is 14 ng/mL in the mid-luteal phase, and with estradiol and inhibin from the corpus luteum it strongly inhibits GnRH, FSH, and LH. Why the others are wrong: A) Progesterone is highest, not low, in this phase. B) FSH is low, not high, in this phase, and the endometrium is not an endocrine source of gonadotropin suppression. D) The endometrium is a target tissue; it does not secrete factors that control pituitary LH.
questions.trap: Remembering that progesterone suppresses gonadotropins only for the LH surge phase and overlooking its role in the luteal phase.

questions.stem: A combined oral contraceptive supplies a steady daily dose of estrogen and progestin. Based on Figure 1, it prevents ovulation mainly because

options.A: it raises FSH and LH continuously, which exhausts the follicles
options.B: it blocks LH receptors on the oocyte, which prevents fertilization
options.C: constant steroid levels maintain negative feedback and prevent the high, sustained estradiol pattern needed for the LH surge
options.D: it increases GnRH pulse frequency, which causes premature luteolysis and prevents the endometrium from supporting implantation of an embryo

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Steady modest steroid levels keep LH and FSH low (like the 50 pg/mL infusion), so follicular development and the surge do not occur. Why the others are wrong: A) Contraceptives lower, not raise, gonadotropins. B) LH acts on granulosa and theca cells, and blocking oocyte receptors is not the mechanism. D) Contraceptives suppress GnRH pulses; they do not raise them.
questions.trap: Believing that hormonal contraceptives work by raising gonadotropins rather than by suppressing them.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, the endometrium reaches its greatest thickness in the mid-luteal phase because

options.A: falling estradiol and progesterone cause the endometrium to proliferate
options.B: FSH acts directly on the endometrium, which causes it to thicken
options.C: the LH surge triggers the endometrium to double in thickness within 24 hours by direct stimulation of uterine stromal cells
options.D: progesterone from the corpus luteum promotes secretory development of an endometrium previously primed by estradiol

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Estradiol drives proliferation in the follicular phase; progesterone then converts the endometrium to a secretory, nutrient-rich state suitable for implantation. Why the others are wrong: A) Falling steroid levels trigger menstruation, not growth. B) FSH acts on ovarian follicles, not on endometrial cells. C) The mid-cycle endometrium is 10 mm, with only a small change from the late follicular phase, so no doubling occurs.
questions.trap: Assigning endometrial growth to pituitary hormones rather than to ovarian steroids.

passages.passage_text: Premature infants are at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) because their lungs are deficient in pulmonary surfactant, a mixture of phospholipids and proteins made by alveolar type II cells. Surfactant lowers the surface tension at the air-liquid interface of the alveoli. Researchers studied lungs excised from preterm lambs. One group had received no treatment, and the other received intratracheal surfactant before delivery. Each lung was inflated to a pressure of 30 cm H2O and then deflated stepwise, and the retained volume was recorded at each pressure. Figure 1 shows the deflation pressure-volume curves, with volume expressed per kilogram of body weight. Compliance was defined as the change in volume divided by the change in pressure over the steep linear portion of each curve, between 5 and 15 cm H2O. Lambs were delivered at 128 days of gestation, which is comparable to about 28 weeks in humans, and lungs were degassed before the pressure-volume measurements began.

graph.title: Figure 1. Deflation pressure-volume curves of preterm lamb lungs

questions.stem: What was the compliance of the surfactant-treated lungs between 5 and 15 cm H2O?

options.A: 0.8 mL/kg per cm H2O
options.B: 3.6 mL/kg per cm H2O
options.C: 2.6 mL/kg per cm H2O
options.D: 26 mL/kg per cm H2O

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Volume rose from 10 to 36 mL/kg (26 mL/kg) over a 10 cm H2O interval, so compliance = 26 / 10 = 2.6 mL/kg per cm H2O. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.8 is the compliance of the untreated lungs ((9 - 1) / 10). B) 3.6 divides the final volume at 15 cm H2O by 10 and ignores the starting volume. D) 26 is the volume change and has not been divided by the pressure change.
questions.trap: Dividing the final volume by the pressure rather than the change in volume by the change in pressure.

questions.stem: According to the Law of Laplace, why does absence of surfactant promote alveolar collapse?

options.A: Pressure in a sphere is proportional to radius, so large alveoli have the highest pressure and collapse first and empty their air into the smaller alveoli that remain open
options.B: Surface tension is unaffected by surfactant, so collapse results only from reduced blood flow
options.C: Collapsing pressure is proportional to surface tension and inversely proportional to radius, so small alveoli empty into larger ones
options.D: Surfactant increases the elastic recoil of the lung, so its absence lowers the collapsing pressure

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Laplace's law (P = 2T/r) shows that, for equal tension, smaller alveoli have a higher collapsing pressure; surfactant reduces T more in small alveoli, stabilizing them. Why the others are wrong: A) Pressure is inversely, not directly, related to radius. B) Surfactant specifically lowers surface tension, which is the point of the passage. D) Surfactant reduces the recoil from surface tension and thus increases compliance, which is opposite to the stated claim.
questions.trap: Reversing the radius relationship in Laplace's law, so that large alveoli appear to be at greatest risk.

questions.stem: Which hormone, given to a mother before preterm delivery, most effectively accelerates surfactant production in the fetal lung?

options.A: A glucocorticoid such as betamethasone
options.B: Oxytocin, to induce contractions and shorten pregnancy
options.C: Progesterone, to maintain the uterine lining
options.D: Epinephrine, to dilate the fetal bronchioles

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Antenatal glucocorticoids induce maturation of type II cells and increase surfactant synthesis, lowering the incidence and severity of RDS. Why the others are wrong: B) Oxytocin does not affect lung maturation and would promote preterm labor. C) Progesterone may delay labor but does not induce surfactant production. D) Epinephrine is a bronchodilator but does not stimulate surfactant synthesis.
questions.trap: Selecting a hormone associated with labor or pregnancy rather than lung maturation.

questions.stem: Compared with a healthy neonate, an infant with RDS is most likely to show

options.A: hyperoxemia caused by reduced alveolar surface tension
options.B: an increased lung compliance, which reduces the work of breathing and improves the ventilation of the alveoli at low pressure
options.C: decreased alveolar-capillary membrane permeability to oxygen
options.D: hypoxemia caused by atelectasis, which leaves perfused alveoli unventilated and produces a right-to-left shunt

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Collapsed alveoli receive blood but no ventilation, so shunted blood remains deoxygenated; stiff lungs also make breathing harder. Why the others are wrong: A) Surfactant deficiency raises, not lowers, surface tension. B) Figure 1 shows the untreated lung has a lower, not higher, compliance. C) The problem is collapse of alveoli, not diffusion across the membrane.
questions.trap: Linking RDS to a diffusion barrier rather than to alveolar collapse and shunt.

questions.stem: What is the most likely reason the surfactant-treated curve flattens between 20 and 30 cm H2O?

options.A: Surfactant is washed away from the alveoli as pressure rises
options.B: The lung approaches its elastic limit, as collagen and elastin fibers resist further stretching
options.C: The alveoli collapse completely at high pressure, which reduces volume
options.D: The airway resistance becomes very high at large volumes, which stops airflow even in a static measurement

questions.explanation: Correct: B) At high volumes the connective tissue limits distensibility, so large pressure changes yield small volume changes, regardless of surface tension. Why the others are wrong: A) Surfactant is not removed by pressure; its effect is largest at low volumes. C) Alveoli collapse at low, not high, pressure. D) The measurements are static and not determined by airway resistance.
questions.trap: Attributing the plateau to surfactant behavior rather than to the elastic properties of the tissue.

passages.passage_text: Natural killer (NK) cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization. NK cells carry inhibitory receptors that bind class I MHC molecules; when class I MHC is abundant, inhibitory signals dominate, and when it is low, activating signals can trigger killing through the release of perforin and granzymes. CD8+ T cells, by contrast, recognize viral peptides presented by class I MHC. Researchers incubated target cells with NK cells or with virus-specific CD8+ T cells at an effector-to-target ratio of 10:1 for 4 hours and measured specific lysis. Surface class I MHC was measured by flow cytometry and expressed relative to uninfected Line A (set to 1.0). K562 is a leukemia line that expresses almost no class I MHC. Virus V is known to reduce class I MHC expression. Results are shown in Table 1. Data are the means of triplicate wells from three independent experiments, and spontaneous release was below 10% in all conditions.

| Line A, uninfected | 1.0 | 5 | 2 |
| Line A infected with virus V | 0.3 | 38 | 18 |

questions.stem: The high NK cell lysis of K562 cells is best explained by

options.A: strong recognition of K562 antigens by NK cell T-cell receptors
options.B: the absence of class I MHC on the target, which removes inhibitory signals to the NK cell
options.C: high class I MHC levels, which activate NK cell killing
options.D: the production of antibodies against K562 by NK cells

questions.explanation: Correct: B) NK cells detect missing self: when class I MHC is nearly absent, inhibitory receptors are not engaged, and activating signals lead to lysis. Why the others are wrong: A) NK cells do not use clonal T-cell receptors. C) High class I MHC inhibits NK cells, as the uninfected Line A result (5%) shows. D) NK cells do not secrete antibodies; B cells do.
questions.trap: Thinking that NK cell activation requires recognition of antigen presented on MHC like a T cell.

questions.stem: What do the results with the Fab fragment of the class I MHC blocking antibody show?

options.A: Masking class I MHC on a normal cell is sufficient to make it susceptible to NK cell lysis
options.B: Class I MHC is required for NK cell perforin production
options.C: Class I MHC is activating for NK cells and increases killing
options.D: CD8+ T cells require NK cells to kill Line A cells

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Lysis by NK cells rose from 5% to 41% when the inhibitory ligand was masked, while CD8+ T cell lysis stayed low (1%). Why the others are wrong: B) The NK cells killed effectively, so perforin was produced when the inhibitory signal was removed. C) Killing went up when class I MHC was blocked, so it is an inhibitory, not an activating, ligand. D) The data show no interaction between NK cells and CD8+ T cells.
questions.trap: Reading the antibody as damaging the cell rather than masking the ligand; a Fab fragment cannot recruit complement or other effectors.

questions.stem: Virus V reduces class I MHC. Based on Table 1, what is the likely advantage and the likely cost for the virus?

options.A: Fewer viral peptides reach NK cells, but the infected cell becomes a stronger CD8+ T cell target
options.B: Fewer viral peptides reach CD8+ T cells, but the infected cell is a stronger NK cell target
options.C: Greater viral antigen display to CD8+ T cells, with no change in NK cell sensitivity
options.D: Reduced NK cell lysis and increased CD8+ T cell lysis because the cell has less class I MHC

questions.explanation: Correct: B) T cell lysis was reduced to 18% and NK cell lysis increased to 38%, a trade-off. Why the others are wrong: A) NK cells do not need peptides; their killing rises when class I MHC falls. C) Lower class I MHC means less peptide display, not more, and NK killing was higher. D) Both predicted effects are reversed relative to the data.
questions.trap: Thinking that lowering class I MHC should help the virus evade every kind of lymphocyte.

questions.stem: A cell line lacks TAP, the transporter that moves peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum, and displays low surface class I MHC. Compared with a normal line, this line would most likely be

options.A: less susceptible to NK cell lysis and more susceptible to CD8+ T cell lysis
options.B: equally susceptible to both cell types because TAP acts after antigen presentation
options.C: more susceptible to NK cell lysis and less to CD8+ T cell lysis
options.D: more susceptible to lysis by both cell types because it cannot degrade antigens

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Without peptide loading, class I MHC is unstable and poorly expressed, which releases NK inhibition and removes the T cell target. Why the others are wrong: A) This reverses both effects. B) TAP acts before presentation and determines how much class I MHC reaches the surface. D) Antigen degradation by the proteasome is unaffected, and low class I MHC reduces T cell recognition.
questions.trap: Overlooking that class I MHC surface expression depends on peptide loading.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes NK cells from CD8+ T cells in this study?

options.A: NK cells use the T-cell receptor and V(D)J recombination to recognize antigens presented on class I MHC
options.B: NK cells need previous infection and develop immunologic memory
options.C: NK cells use Fas ligand only, and not perforin and granzymes
options.D: NK cells kill without clonal selection or previous exposure, so they can act within hours

questions.explanation: Correct: D) NK cells are part of innate immunity and use germline-encoded receptors, whereas CD8+ T cells require clonal expansion for specificity. Why the others are wrong: A) NK cells do not rearrange receptor genes. B) Immunologic memory is a characteristic of adaptive cells. C) NK cells use perforin and granzymes as stated in the passage.
questions.trap: Treating NK cells as a type of T cell with antigen-specific receptors.

passages.passage_text: Long-term potentiation (LTP), a persistent strengthening of synapses after brief high-frequency activity, is a leading cellular model of memory. In hippocampal slices, a pathway of Schaffer collaterals onto CA1 neurons was stimulated at low frequency while the field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP) slope was recorded and expressed as a percentage of baseline. At time 0, a brief high-frequency tetanus was delivered. In control slices, the fEPSP stayed elevated. Other slices were bathed in APV, an antagonist of the NMDA receptor, or in anisomycin, an inhibitor of protein synthesis, beginning 20 minutes before the tetanus. Figure 1 shows fEPSP slope over four hours. NMDA receptors are blocked at resting potential by Mg2+ and become permeable to Ca2+ when glutamate is bound and the membrane is depolarized. Slices were maintained at 32 degrees C in oxygenated artificial cerebrospinal fluid, and responses were recorded from the stratum radiatum of CA1. The tetanus consisted of 100 pulses at 100 Hz.

graph.title: Figure 1. fEPSP slope after a tetanus delivered at time 0

questions.stem: Why does APV prevent LTP in these experiments?

options.A: APV blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, which prevents the action potential in the presynaptic terminal and therefore stops the release of glutamate from the Schaffer collaterals
options.B: NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors that allow Ca2+ entry only when glutamate binding and postsynaptic depolarization occur together
options.C: APV blocks the presynaptic release of glutamate, which means the tetanus is not transmitted
options.D: APV blocks AMPA receptors, which prevents any baseline fEPSP before the tetanus

questions.explanation: Correct: B) NMDA receptor-mediated Ca2+ entry triggers LTP; blocking it leaves baseline transmission intact but prevents the potentiation (fEPSP stays near 100%). Why the others are wrong: A) Na+ channel blockade would eliminate baseline transmission, but the baseline was unchanged. C) APV acts on postsynaptic NMDA receptors and does not alter glutamate release. D) Baseline fEPSP was normal before the tetanus, which AMPA receptors would not allow if they were blocked.
questions.trap: Assuming that the antagonist blocks all glutamatergic transmission instead of only the NMDA receptor component.

questions.stem: Which postsynaptic change most directly increases the fEPSP during the first hour after the tetanus?

options.A: Ca2+ activates CaMKII, which promotes insertion and phosphorylation of AMPA receptors in the postsynaptic membrane
options.B: Ca2+ activates acetylcholinesterase, which increases the clearance of glutamate
options.C: Ca2+ closes the NMDA receptor channels permanently, which prevents desensitization and limits further Ca2+ entry during the tetanus
options.D: Ca2+ activates voltage-gated Cl- channels, which depolarize the postsynaptic cell

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Early LTP is expressed as more and more active AMPA receptors, increasing the response to a given quantity of glutamate. Why the others are wrong: B) Faster glutamate clearance would reduce, not increase, the response. C) The channel isn't closed permanently, and the response increased. D) Cl- channels would hyperpolarize or clamp the membrane near the Cl- equilibrium potential.
questions.trap: Proposing a presynaptic or glial change for an effect that the data localize to the postsynaptic neuron.

questions.stem: Anisomycin produced a significant divergence from control beginning at about 60 minutes. These data best support the conclusion that

options.A: early LTP does not require new protein synthesis, whereas maintenance of potentiation for hours does
options.B: LTP induction needs protein synthesis, because potentiation was reduced at 10 minutes
options.C: protein synthesis is needed only for the baseline response before the tetanus
options.D: anisomycin blocks NMDA receptors, as APV does

questions.explanation: Correct: A) At 10 and 30 minutes anisomycin slices matched control (188 and 172 versus 190 and 180), but the potentiation decayed to baseline by 240 minutes. Why the others are wrong: B) Potentiation at 10 minutes was almost identical to control (188 versus 190), so induction was intact. C) Baseline was not altered by anisomycin before the tetanus. D) Anisomycin allowed an initial LTP, whereas APV prevented it, so their mechanisms differ.
questions.trap: Reading any drug effect as a block of induction without comparing the early time points.

questions.stem: In the control slices, what fraction of the initial potentiation (the increase above baseline at 10 minutes) remained at 240 minutes?

options.A: About 55%
options.B: About 87%
options.C: About 72%
options.D: About 165%

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Initial potentiation was 190 - 100 = 90 points; at 240 minutes it was 165 - 100 = 65 points; 65 / 90 is approximately 0.72. Why the others are wrong: A) 55% would correspond to a drop to about 150%. B) 87% results from dividing 165 by 190, which does not subtract the baseline. D) 165% is the fEPSP value itself rather than a fraction of potentiation.
questions.trap: Dividing raw fEPSP values without subtracting the 100% baseline.

questions.stem: A patient with bilateral damage to the hippocampus is most likely to show which deficit?

options.A: Loss of all memories from before the injury, with preserved ability to form new ones
options.B: Loss of the ability to learn new motor skills but preservation of declarative memory
options.C: Loss of language comprehension, with no effect on memory formation
options.D: Inability to form new explicit (declarative) memories, while previously learned motor skills remain intact

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The hippocampus is needed for consolidating new declarative memories, as in patient H.M.; procedural learning depends on other structures. Why the others are wrong: A) This describes retrograde amnesia, which is not the typical pattern for hippocampal damage. B) This reverses the roles: procedural memory is spared by hippocampal damage. C) Language comprehension is mainly a function of Wernicke's area in the temporal cortex.
questions.trap: Confusing anterograde amnesia from hippocampal damage with retrograde amnesia.

passages.passage_text: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix and requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a cofactor of its E1 subunit. Lactic acidosis can arise from impaired PDC activity or from defects of the respiratory chain. Cultured fibroblasts were grown under four conditions, and PDC activity was assayed in lysates with and without added 1 mM TPP. Lactate and pyruvate in the culture medium were also measured. The lactate-to-pyruvate (L/P) ratio reflects the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio because lactate dehydrogenase equilibrates the two couples. Results are in Table 1. The E1 variant cells carry a missense mutation in the E1 subunit. Cells were cultured in glucose-containing medium for 48 hours before analysis, and lysates were prepared with detergent to release mitochondrial enzymes. Thiamine-depleted cells were grown in thiamine-free medium for two weeks, and the complex I defect arose from a mutation in a subunit of that complex. All assays were done in triplicate.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Control | 12.0 | 12.4 | 1.0 | 0.10 | 10 |
| Thiamine-depleted | 3.0 | 11.5 | 4.2 | 0.35 | 12 |
| E1 variant | 2.5 | 10.8 | 4.0 | 0.30 | 13 |
| Complex I defect | 11.5 | 11.9 | 5.0 | 0.12 | 42 |

questions.stem: Which set of cofactors is required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex as a whole?

options.A: Biotin, lipoic acid, FAD, NADP+, and coenzyme A, with ATP as the energy source
options.B: Thiamine pyrophosphate, pyridoxal phosphate, FMN, NAD+, and ATP
options.C: Biotin, thiamine pyrophosphate, FAD, NADPH, and tetrahydrofolate
options.D: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+, and coenzyme A

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The E1, E2, and E3 subunits use TPP, lipoamide, and FAD, respectively, with NAD+ as the final electron acceptor and CoA as the acyl acceptor. Why the others are wrong: A) Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylases and is not used by PDC, and NADP+ is not the acceptor. B) Pyridoxal phosphate is used in transamination, and ATP is not a cofactor. C) Biotin and tetrahydrofolate are not PDC cofactors, and NADH, not NADPH, is generated.
questions.trap: Mixing up the cofactors of PDC with those of the carboxylases or transaminases.

questions.stem: Why does lactate accumulate in the thiamine-depleted cells?

options.A: Lactate is formed from acetyl-CoA, which accumulates when PDC is overactive
options.B: Without PDC activity, gluconeogenesis converts glucose to lactate in the matrix
options.C: Reduced PDC activity lets pyruvate build up and be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates NAD+
options.D: Lactate dehydrogenase is inhibited when PDC activity is low, so lactate stays in the cell and is not released into the medium

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Pyruvate not oxidized by PDC is diverted to lactate; in these cells the L/P ratio is nearly unchanged (12), so the excess is of both metabolites. Why the others are wrong: A) PDC activity was lower, not higher, and acetyl-CoA is not a lactate precursor. B) Gluconeogenesis builds glucose, not lactate, and does not occur in the matrix of fibroblasts. D) If LDH were inhibited, lactate would fall rather than rise.
questions.trap: Assuming that lactic acidosis always signals an elevated NADH/NAD+ ratio rather than a pyruvate surplus.

questions.stem: The L/P ratio is 42 in the complex I-defective cells but 10 to 13 in the other cells. This difference is best explained by

options.A: increased pyruvate carboxylase activity in the matrix, which converts lactate to pyruvate and lowers the NADH/NAD+ ratio in the cytosol
options.B: enhanced thiamine uptake, which drives pyruvate into acetyl-CoA
options.C: an inability to take up glucose, which decreases pyruvate levels
options.D: impaired reoxidation of NADH in mitochondria, which raises the NADH/NAD+ ratio and drives lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate

questions.explanation: Correct: D) A complex I defect leaves NADH unoxidized, which raises NADH/NAD+ and favors lactate over pyruvate; PDC itself is normal (11.5). Why the others are wrong: A) Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate, not lactate to pyruvate. B) Thiamine would raise PDC flux and lower lactate, but PDC activity is normal here. C) Glucose uptake is not limited; pyruvate is 0.12 mM and lactate is high.
questions.trap: Treating all lactic acidosis as the same disorder, ignoring what the L/P ratio says about redox state.

questions.stem: The E1 variant cells recovered most of their PDC activity with 1 mM TPP. The most likely explanation is that the mutation

options.A: destroys the catalytic site of E1, so that no amount of cofactor restores activity
options.B: increases the production of E1 mRNA, so excess TPP is required for degradation
options.C: blocks entry of pyruvate into the mitochondria, so TPP bypasses the transporter
options.D: lowers the affinity of E1 for TPP, so excess cofactor restores saturation

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Activity rose from 2.5 to 10.8 nmol/min/mg, consistent with a higher Km for TPP overcome by raising the cofactor concentration; such patients may respond to high-dose thiamine. Why the others are wrong: A) A destroyed catalytic site would not show an almost fourfold recovery with TPP. B) Higher E1 mRNA would not be corrected by TPP and does not fit the lysate assay. C) The lysate assay does not depend on the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier.
questions.trap: Assuming any loss of enzyme activity must be irreversible instead of considering cofactor binding.

passages.passage_text: In Xenopus egg extracts, the cell cycle can be driven in a test tube. Entry into mitosis requires activation of the cyclin B-CDK1 complex, and exit requires the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C) to ubiquitinate cyclin B for proteasomal degradation. In a time course, extracts containing sperm nuclei were sampled every 20 minutes for cyclin B level and for histone H1 kinase activity, a readout of CDK1 activity (Figure 1; both normalized to the peak value). In additional extracts, sampled at 100 minutes, researchers added either a mutant cyclin B that lacks the destruction box recognized by the APC/C (cyclin B-delta90) or the CDK inhibitor roscovitine. The fraction of nuclei with condensed chromosomes was scored (Table 1). Extracts were prepared from eggs arrested in metaphase of meiosis II and then released by calcium addition, so that they cycled in vitro through repeated rounds of interphase and mitosis at 23 degrees C. Chromosomes were visualized with a DNA dye.

|---|---|---|---|
| Control | 0.3 | 0.10 | 6 |
| + cyclin B-delta90 | 1.0 | 1.00 | 92 |
| + roscovitine | 0.9 | 0.04 | 3 |

graph.title: Figure 1. Cyclin B level and H1 kinase activity in control extract

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of the drop in both cyclin B and kinase activity between 60 and 80 minutes in the control extract?

options.A: Activation of CDK1 by degradation of its catalytic subunit at the end of S phase
options.B: Translation of cyclin B is inhibited by roscovitine, so that CDK1 remains inactive
options.C: Phosphorylation of cyclin B by CDK1 stabilizes the protein and shuts down the cycle
options.D: APC/C destroys cyclin B, which inactivates CDK1 and permits exit from mitosis

questions.explanation: Correct: D) CDK1 requires cyclin B for activity; degradation by the APC/C removes the regulatory subunit, and kinase activity falls with it. Why the others are wrong: A) CDK1 is not degraded in this process; the cyclin is. B) Roscovitine was not added to the control extract. C) Stabilizing cyclin B would keep kinase activity high, not turn it off.
questions.trap: Thinking that the catalytic CDK subunit, not the cyclin, is the one destroyed at each cycle.

questions.stem: Cells in the roscovitine extract accumulate cyclin B (0.9) but do not condense chromosomes. This shows that

options.A: cyclin B is the catalytic kinase that phosphorylates histone H1 and nuclear lamins, so its presence alone drives condensation
options.B: cyclin B alone is insufficient; the kinase activity of CDK1 is needed to drive chromosome condensation
options.C: roscovitine increases the rate of cyclin B degradation
options.D: chromosome condensation is independent of the cell cycle

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Roscovitine inhibits CDK1, so kinase activity (0.04) is low despite high cyclin B, and condensation (3%) fails; the CDK is the catalytic subunit. Why the others are wrong: A) Cyclins are regulatory and have no catalytic activity of their own. C) Degradation was not increased; cyclin B in this extract remained high. D) Condensation was driven by CDK1 activity, so it is dependent on the cycle.
questions.trap: Assuming that the level of cyclin by itself reports the kinase activity.

questions.stem: The extract containing cyclin B-delta90 arrests with condensed chromosomes (92%). This outcome indicates that

options.A: destruction of cyclin B is needed to enter mitosis
options.B: CDK1 activity is required for completion of DNA replication but not for mitosis
options.C: CDK1 activity is sufficient to enter mitosis, but cyclin B destruction is needed to exit it
options.D: the delta90 mutant cyclin B inhibits the proteasome and stops the cell in G1

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The non-degradable cyclin keeps CDK1 active (1.00), driving and holding the mitotic state. Why the others are wrong: A) The control shows cyclin B accumulating before mitosis, not being destroyed. B) Condensation shows mitosis was entered, which is a function of CDK1. D) A non-degradable cyclin lacks the recognition site, but it does not inhibit the proteasome, and cells were in mitosis, not G1.
questions.trap: Reading mitotic arrest as a failure to enter mitosis.

questions.stem: In the control extract, by what factor was kinase activity at 60 minutes greater than at 100 minutes?

options.A: About 0.1
options.B: About 3.3
options.C: About 90
options.D: About 9.5

questions.explanation: Correct: D) At 60 minutes the activity was 0.95 and at 100 minutes it was 0.10; 0.95 / 0.10 = 9.5. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.1 would be the ratio of the 100-minute value to the 60-minute value, which is the inverse. B) 3.3 comes from dividing the cyclin B levels (1.0 / 0.3). C) 90 results from a decimal error, since 0.95 / 0.10 is not 90.
questions.trap: Inverting the ratio, or comparing cyclin B levels instead of kinase activity.

passages.passage_text: Ethanol is metabolized mainly in the liver. Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, and mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate; each step reduces NAD+ to NADH. About 40% of people of East Asian ancestry carry the ALDH2*2 allele, which encodes a nearly inactive enzyme. Healthy adult volunteers received either placebo or ethanol (0.5 g/kg). Blood was sampled 4 hours later. Participants were studied either after an overnight fast or after a meal, and a group heterozygous for ALDH2*2 was included. Plasma glucose, lactate, lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio, and acetaldehyde are shown in Table 1. Ethanol was given as a drink over 20 minutes, and peak blood ethanol concentrations were similar in all groups. Participants abstained from alcohol for one week before testing. The fed groups consumed a standard mixed meal containing about 600 kcal 30 minutes before the drink. Acetaldehyde was measured by gas chromatography. Each participant was studied once.

questions.stem: Why did fasted volunteers develop hypoglycemia after ethanol?

options.A: Ethanol stimulates insulin secretion strongly, which causes the liver to store glucose as glycogen and the muscle to take up the remaining glucose from blood
options.B: The high NADH/NAD+ ratio diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, which lowers the substrates available for gluconeogenesis
options.C: Ethanol inhibits glycogen phosphorylase directly, which raises glucose uptake by muscle
options.D: Acetaldehyde is converted to glucose in the liver, which uses up the available glucose

questions.explanation: Correct: B) In the fasted state glucose is supplied by gluconeogenesis; NADH from ethanol oxidation shifts the LDH and malate dehydrogenase equilibria away from pyruvate and oxaloacetate, and glucose falls to 58 mg/dL. Why the others are wrong: A) Insulin secretion is not the main mechanism; the fed group, which had glycogen available, did not become hypoglycemic. C) Glycogen phosphorylase is not the target; the fasted state has depleted glycogen and relies on gluconeogenesis. D) Acetaldehyde is oxidized to acetate and does not form glucose.
questions.trap: Attributing alcohol-induced hypoglycemia to insulin rather than to redox-impaired gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem: In the ALDH2*1/*2 group, plasma acetaldehyde was 45 uM, 15 times that of ALDH2*1/*1 participants. The most likely explanation is that

options.A: the variant allele increases ADH activity, which lowers the production of acetaldehyde
options.B: the variant allele blocks the formation of acetaldehyde from ethanol, which leaves ethanol unmetabolized and lowers the plasma acetaldehyde concentration
options.C: the variant ALDH2 subunits reduce the oxidation of acetaldehyde to acetate, so acetaldehyde accumulates after ADH makes it
options.D: acetaldehyde cannot be filtered by the kidney in heterozygous carriers

questions.explanation: Correct: C) ALDH2 is the main acetaldehyde-clearing enzyme; reduced activity leaves it elevated, which produces facial flushing and nausea. Lactate and L/P values were similar to wild type, so NADH generation by ADH was unaffected. Why the others are wrong: A) A higher ADH activity would raise, not lower, acetaldehyde production. B) If acetaldehyde formation were blocked, acetaldehyde would be low. D) Renal filtration is not the main route of acetaldehyde clearance.
questions.trap: Choosing a step upstream of acetaldehyde rather than the enzyme that removes it.

questions.stem: In the fasted ethanol group with a lactate of 2.8 mM and an L/P ratio of 28, the pyruvate concentration was approximately

options.D: 78 mM

questions.explanation: Correct: B) L/P = 28, so pyruvate = lactate / 28 = 2.8 / 28 = 0.10 mM. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.01 mM results from a tenfold arithmetic error. C) 0.36 mM is the reciprocal of the lactate value (1 / 2.8) and ignores the ratio. D) 78 mM is the product of 2.8 and 28, which multiplies instead of divides.
questions.trap: Multiplying lactate by the ratio instead of dividing.

questions.stem: High hepatic NADH/NAD+ after heavy ethanol use contributes to fatty liver mainly because it

options.A: inhibits beta-oxidation of fatty acids and favors triglyceride synthesis
options.B: stimulates beta-oxidation, which raises acetyl-CoA, and thereby depletes triglycerides
options.C: activates the pentose phosphate pathway, which generates NADPH and degrades fatty acids
options.D: increases carnitine uptake into mitochondria, which accelerates fatty acid oxidation

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Oxidation steps in beta-oxidation and the TCA cycle need NAD+, so excess NADH slows them; fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides that accumulate in hepatocytes. Why the others are wrong: B) Beta-oxidation is slowed, not stimulated, when NAD+ is scarce. C) The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH for biosynthesis and does not degrade fatty acids. D) Faster mitochondrial oxidation would reduce fat accumulation, the opposite of what occurs.
questions.trap: Thinking more NADH means more fuel oxidation, when it actually inhibits NAD+-dependent steps.

discrete.stem: A tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Ala is placed in an electric field at pH 7.4. Which statement best describes its net charge and migration?

options.A: Net charge of +1, migrating toward the cathode
options.B: Net charge of 0, with no migration in the field
options.C: Net charge of -2, toward the anode
options.D: Net charge of -3, migrating toward the anode

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) At pH 7.4 the N-terminal amine is +1, the C-terminal carboxylate -1, and the Glu and Asp side chains -1 each, for a net of -2; negative species move toward the anode. Why the others are wrong: A) The side chains of Glu and Asp are deprotonated at pH 7.4, so the peptide is not positive. B) Only a zwitterion with balanced charges would be neutral, and the two acidic side chains prevent that. D) The N-terminal amine contributes +1, so the net charge is -2 rather than -3.
discrete.trap: Counting only the three carboxylate groups and forgetting the positive N-terminus.

discrete.stem: A protein migrates as a single band of 60 kDa on a nonreducing SDS-PAGE gel but as two bands of 35 kDa and 25 kDa after treatment with beta-mercaptoethanol. The protein is most likely

options.A: a homodimer held together by noncovalent hydrophobic interactions between two identical subunits
options.B: a heterodimer whose two different subunits are linked by an interchain disulfide bond
options.C: a single polypeptide with an intrachain disulfide bond
options.D: a monomer cleaved by the reducing agent at peptide bonds

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) A reducing agent breaks disulfide bonds; two unequal bands that sum to the intact size show two different chains joined by a disulfide. Why the others are wrong: A) SDS disrupts noncovalent interactions, so a noncovalent homodimer would not run as 60 kDa and would give equal bands. C) An intrachain disulfide would give one band on both gels. D) Reducing agents cleave disulfide bonds, not peptide bonds.
discrete.trap: Forgetting that SDS dissociates noncovalent assemblies, so a persistent larger band implies covalent linkage.

discrete.stem: A drug inhibits DNA ligase in dividing cells. Which result is most expected immediately after treatment?

options.A: Accumulation of RNA primers on the leading strand
options.B: Failure of helicase to unwind the origin of replication
options.C: Loss of the 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading of DNA polymerase III
options.D: Accumulation of short Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments after primer removal, so inhibiting it leaves unjoined fragments on the lagging strand. Why the others are wrong: A) The leading strand is made continuously with a single primer and does not rely on ligase for continuity. B) Helicase acts before ligase and is not dependent on it. C) Proofreading is a polymerase function and is unaffected by ligase inhibition.
discrete.trap: Applying a ligase block to the leading strand, which is synthesized continuously.

discrete.stem: An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 2,500 newborns in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the approximate frequency of carriers?
discrete.explanation: Correct: C) q squared = 1/2,500 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02 and p = 0.98; carriers are 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.039. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.0004 is the frequency of affected individuals (q squared), not carriers. B) 0.020 is the allele frequency q, not the carrier frequency. D) 0.980 is the frequency of the normal allele p.
discrete.trap: Reporting the allele frequency q instead of calculating 2pq.

discrete.stem: Complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of myristic acid (14 carbons, saturated) yields which products?

options.A: 7 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2, and 7 NADH
options.B: 14 acetyl-CoA, 6 FADH2, and 6 NADH
options.C: 7 acetyl-CoA, 6 FADH2, 6 NADH
options.D: 6 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH2, and 7 NADH

discrete.explanation: Correct: C) A 14-carbon fatty acid gives 14/2 = 7 acetyl-CoA, and it requires 7 - 1 = 6 rounds of oxidation, each producing one FADH2 and one NADH. Why the others are wrong: A) The final round releases two acetyl-CoA, so only 6 FADH2 and NADH are made. B) Each acetyl-CoA contains two carbons, so 14 carbons yield 7 acetyl-CoA rather than 14. D) Six rounds of oxidation yield 7 acetyl-CoA, not 6, and 6 FADH2 and NADH.
discrete.trap: Setting the number of cycles equal to the number of acetyl-CoA molecules.

discrete.stem: In I-cell disease, lysosomal enzymes are found in the extracellular fluid instead of in lysosomes. Which defect best explains this finding?

options.A: Failure to add mannose-6-phosphate to lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi apparatus, which prevents sorting to lysosomes
options.B: Failure to add a signal sequence to enzymes, which prevents entry into the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the secretory pathway
options.C: Failure to acidify lysosomes, which prevents the activity of hydrolases
options.D: Failure of the peroxisome to import enzymes containing a PTS1 sequence

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi and recognized by receptors that carry them to lysosomes; without the tag, they default to secretion. Why the others are wrong: B) Without a signal sequence, the enzymes would not be made in the rough ER and would not be secreted. C) Poor acidification would reduce enzyme activity but would not move enzymes outside the cell. D) Peroxisomal import defects affect peroxisomal enzymes, not lysosomal ones.
discrete.trap: Choosing a defect in ER entry for a problem with Golgi sorting.

discrete.stem: A donor Hfr E. coli cell is mixed with an F- recipient. After brief mixing, the recipient most likely

options.A: receives part of the donor chromosome but remains F- because the F factor is transferred last
options.B: becomes F+ because the F factor is the first segment of DNA to be transferred during the mating
options.C: receives the whole donor chromosome and becomes Hfr
options.D: acquires only the F plasmid and no chromosomal genes

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) In an Hfr cell the F factor is integrated into the chromosome; transfer starts within the integrated factor and the rest of F enters last, so mating usually breaks before it reaches the recipient. Why the others are wrong: B) F+ conversion occurs with F+ donors, not Hfr, because the F genes are at the end of the transferred DNA. C) Complete chromosome transfer would need about 100 minutes of undisturbed contact and is rare. D) Transfer of the chromosome, not of an F plasmid, is what characterizes Hfr matings.
discrete.trap: Confusing Hfr matings with F+ by F plasmid transfer.

discrete.stem: Which of the following tissues is derived from embryonic endoderm?

options.A: The epidermis of the skin
options.B: The smooth muscle of the intestinal wall
options.C: The adrenal medulla
options.D: The epithelial lining of the trachea and lungs

discrete.explanation: Correct: D) The epithelium of the respiratory tract and the gut forms from endoderm, whereas muscle, blood, and bone come from mesoderm. Why the others are wrong: A) The epidermis is formed from ectoderm. B) Smooth muscle is derived from mesoderm. C) The adrenal medulla comes from neural crest cells, which are of ectodermal origin.
discrete.trap: Assigning organs by the location of the tissue rather than by embryonic germ layer.

discrete.stem: A patient takes atropine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist. Compared with the resting state before the drug, which change is most likely?

options.A: A decrease in resting heart rate, because sympathetic input is blocked
options.B: An increase in resting heart rate, because vagal slowing of the SA node is blocked
options.C: No change in heart rate, because the SA node is regulated by hormones only
options.D: A decrease in resting heart rate, because parasympathetic input is enhanced

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) At rest the vagus nerve releases acetylcholine on M2 receptors, which slows the SA node; blocking this removes vagal tone and raises the rate. Why the others are wrong: A) Atropine does not block adrenergic receptors; sympathetic input is unchanged. C) The SA node is under dominant parasympathetic tone at rest, so blocking it changes the rate. D) Atropine antagonizes the receptor and does not enhance parasympathetic action.
discrete.trap: Assuming that a muscarinic antagonist should slow the heart because it is called an autonomic drug.

discrete.stem: A woman with a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Treatment with a dopamine agonist is effective because dopamine

options.A: stimulates prolactin release from the hypothalamus, which lowers LH
options.B: inhibits prolactin release from lactotrophs, which lowers prolactin and restores GnRH secretion
options.C: inhibits oxytocin release, which prevents milk letdown
options.D: stimulates GnRH, which directly shrinks the tumor

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Hypothalamic dopamine is the prolactin-inhibiting factor; high prolactin suppresses GnRH, so lowering it restores menstruation. Why the others are wrong: A) The hypothalamus does not release prolactin, and dopamine does not stimulate it. C) Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary and is not the target. D) Dopamine does not shrink tumors through GnRH.
discrete.trap: Remembering that dopamine inhibits most pituitary hormones but missing that, for prolactin, tonic hypothalamic input is inhibitory.

discrete.stem: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deeply and rapidly. This pattern is best explained as

options.A: respiratory compensation that raises arterial PCO2 and thereby lowers blood pH
options.B: respiratory compensation that lowers arterial PCO2 and thereby raises blood pH toward normal
options.C: a renal response that increases the excretion of bicarbonate
options.D: a primary respiratory alkalosis caused by a pulmonary disease

discrete.explanation: Correct: B) Metabolic acidosis lowers pH and stimulates chemoreceptors, so hyperventilation blows off CO2 and shifts pH back up. Why the others are wrong: A) Raising PCO2 would worsen the acidosis. C) Excreting bicarbonate would worsen the acidosis; the kidney would conserve it. D) The ventilation pattern is a response to acidosis, not a primary lung disorder.
discrete.trap: Calling the hyperventilation a primary disorder instead of a compensation for metabolic acidosis.

discrete.stem: In the small intestine, which enzyme activates trypsinogen to trypsin and thereby starts the cascade of pancreatic zymogen activation?

options.A: Enteropeptidase, from the duodenal brush border
options.B: Pepsin, secreted by the chief cells of the stomach
options.C: Chymotrypsin, secreted by the acinar cells of the pancreas
options.D: Amylase, secreted by the salivary glands and pancreas

discrete.explanation: Correct: A) Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) cleaves trypsinogen at the duodenal surface; trypsin then activates other zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen. Why the others are wrong: B) Pepsin works in the acidic stomach and does not activate trypsinogen. C) Chymotrypsin is itself activated by trypsin and does not activate trypsinogen. D) Amylase digests starch and does not cleave proteins.
discrete.trap: Picking a pancreatic protease rather than the brush-border enzyme that initiates the cascade.
